summary: The Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) effort aims to complement ingress filtering with finer-grained, standardized IP source address validation. This document describes threats enabled by source address spoofing, reviews current solutions and challenges, and begins an analysis of host-level anti-spoofing work.

eli5.summary: Liars can write a fake return address on messages. This lists the trouble that causes and starts thinking about checking every sender's address.

questions: how do i detect spoofed ip addresses
how do i validate ip addresses on my network
subtitle: Threats from IP source address spoofing and validation strategies

tldr.problem: IP source address spoofing enables various network attacks because the Internet Protocol does not inherently validate whether a packet's source address matches the actual sender.
tldr.mechanism: SAVI aims to complement network ingress filtering (BCP 38) with finer-grained, standardized IP source address validation at the host level and link level, binding IP addresses to network topology or Layer 2 addresses.
tldr.outcome: Host-level validation can prevent internal spoofing attacks, improve traceability of security incidents, and help respond to external attacks more effectively than ingress filtering alone.

today: RFC 6959 is an Informational document that remains active. It serves as the threat scope definition for the broader SAVI standardization effort, which has produced protocols for DHCPv4-based, DHCPv6-based, and SLAAC-based address validation in switched networks.

sections.title: Overview of Source Address Spoofing
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol operates on a connectionless, hop-by-hop forwarding model. Hosts generate IP packets with source and destination addresses, but at the IP layer there is no required transactional state or tracking of which hosts are using the network. This design benefit has a security cost: hosts can forge the source address of packets they transmit, and the network cannot easily tell that the information is false.

Source address validation is necessary to detect and reject spoofed IP packets and improve overall network security. The SAVI effort targets standardized, finer-grained validation that networks can deploy locally for immediate local benefit, complementing broad ingress filtering practices described in BCP 38.

While BCP 38 provides network-layer ingress filtering at Internet boundaries, its effectiveness depends on widespread deployment and it operates only at subnetwork boundaries. SAVI enables local application of address validation at enterprise and access network levels, providing detection of spoofing within LAN environments where multiple hosts share network infrastructure, and enabling rapid response when spoofed traffic is detected.
sections.eli5: The Internet was designed to be simple and fast, so it does not check who really sent a message. Bad guys can pretend to be someone else by lying about their address, and this causes trouble.

sections.title: Attack Vectors Enabled by Spoofing
sections.content:
Two broad classes of spoofing-based attacks exist: blind attacks and non-blind attacks.

Blind attacks occur when the attacker is not on the same LAN as the target and has no access to the data path between attack source and target. These include single-packet DoS attacks (such as LAND attacks that cause target system crashes), RST probe attacks that reset TCP connections, flood-based DoS attacks that overwhelm targets with traffic, poisoning attacks (ARP cache poisoning, ICMP redirects, DNS poisoning), spoof-based worm propagation, reflective amplification attacks (DNS amplification where a single spoofed packet causes large response traffic to a victim), and Smurf attacks using spoofed ICMP echo requests.

Non-blind attacks involve attackers with access to the data path or ability to observe responses. Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks use spoofed ARP or IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages to redirect local traffic. Connection hijacking uses spoofed TCP RST packets with guessed sequence numbers. Third-party reconnaissance uses spoofed source addresses to probe target systems and determine firewall policies.

In local LAN environments, one host may spoof the source addresses of other hosts on the same subnet, enabling attacks that could hijack secure sessions, redirect traffic, or distribute malware without being traced to the actual attacker.
sections.eli5: Attackers can fake sender addresses to crash computers, steal connections, flood networks with traffic, or trick routers and switches into sending traffic the wrong way.

sections.title: Current Anti-Spoofing Solutions
sections.content:
BCP 38 ingress filtering is the primary existing defense, implemented at ISP edges to prevent spoofed prefixes from leaving a network. However, it does not prevent spoofing within a network and requires ubiquitous deployment for effectiveness.

Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) automates BCP 38 filtering by using routing tables to verify that the source address comes from a direction where it would be rational to send a response. Strict uRPF requires the source address to match the interface from which a reply would be sent. Loose uRPF merely checks that the source is routable. Limitations include handling of asymmetric routing and inability to detect spoofing within the same subnet.

Port-based address binding creates associations between IP addresses and network attachment points. Manual binding statically configures which IP addresses are allowed on which switch ports, practical for small networks with static topologies. Automated binding uses DHCP snooping (IPv4) or Duplicate Address Detection observation (IPv6 SLAAC) to dynamically create port-MAC-IP bindings as addresses are allocated. IEEE 802.1x authentication can serve as a binding anchor to verify user authorization before allowing traffic.

Cryptographic techniques like IPsec and DNSSEC provide strong authentication for specific protocols but are not universally deployed. ARP lacks built-in security; Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) provides equivalent for IPv6 but has limited deployment.
sections.eli5: Several methods exist: checking at the edge of the Internet, using routing tables to verify addresses, manually listing which addresses are allowed on each port, or using encryption to prove who you are.

sections.title: Topological and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
Address provisioning introduces complexity because most networks use dynamic allocation via DHCP, DHCPv6, or IPv6 SLAAC rather than static configuration. Port-MAC-IP binding mechanisms must accommodate these dynamic protocols.

Devices with multiple addresses complicate enforcement. Routers and firewalls legitimately originate and forward packets from multiple IP addresses across multiple interfaces, making it impractical to pre-define which addresses are allowed on their ports. NATs forward traffic from many source addresses. Multi-instance hosts (blade servers, virtual machines) create multiple logical hosts per physical port, each with its own IP and MAC addresses, requiring enforcement points within the device.

Multi-LAN hosts with multiple network interfaces may legitimately send packets with different source addresses from different interfaces, or even use loopback addresses, creating false positives if port-MAC-IP bindings are too strict.

Mobile IP and host mobility (virtual machine migration) can move IP addresses to new physical locations, requiring dynamic update of SAVI state on switches.

IPv6 considerations introduce additional challenges. Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) allows hosts to autonomously configure addresses without control-plane interaction, complicating binding establishment. The large 64-bit Interface Identifier space allows hosts to mint many addresses, potentially overwhelming neighbor discovery tables if not rate-limited. Privacy addresses (temporary addresses) complicate logging and attribution.
sections.eli5: Some devices need many addresses, addresses change when they move, and IPv6 lets computers create addresses on their own without asking permission, making it hard to track everything.

sections.title: Host-Level Anti-Spoofing Analysis
sections.content:
Host-level source address validation provides benefits even in complex topologies. Masquerade prevention stops one machine from pretending to be another on the same LAN, preventing hijacking of secure sessions and attacks on routing systems. Because security experts report that most breaches are internal, preventing internal spoofing is valuable.

Incident traceability improves dramatically with host-level validation. When a security incident occurs, address usage tied to network topology anchors (switch ports, MAC addresses) enables rapid determination of which machine on the network is the actual source, faster and more reliable than analyzing ongoing traffic. This is particularly important when an attack originates from within the enterprise.

Global benefits become possible if address usage is tied to network anchors. Large-scale anonymous IPv6 address attacks can be prevented or at least traced to their source machine rather than appearing as distributed attacks.

Host-level enforcement may not achieve complete protection in all topologies (for example, with conventional SLAAC in switched networks where enforcement is only on routers), but even partial protection provides value. The level of achievable protection depends on the specific topology, address allocation mechanisms, and enforcement points chosen.
sections.eli5: Checking addresses at the host level stops computers on the same network from faking each other's addresses, and helps find where attacks really come from much faster than looking at traffic later.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Source address validation alone cannot authenticate the origin of packets. The IP source address, even if validated as legitimate for its network location, does not prove which user or application sent it. Only cryptographic authentication mechanisms like IPsec provide unquestionable source validation.

Even with source address validation deployed, failure modes exist. Inside attackers may probe the network to find spoofing modes that evade detection. To avoid giving false sense of security, network administrators must assume that validation mechanisms may have bypass techniques and monitor for deliberate probing.

Privacy implications of address binding enforcement are significant. Recording IP address bindings may constitute personally identifying information. In many jurisdictions this brings ethical and legal obligations. Collection and retention of logged binding information must be carefully planned.

Binding logs should be removed after binding lifetimes expire to avoid unnecessary privacy exposure. Logs of spoof attempts may require longer retention to detect patterns, but this creates privacy risks. Network administrators collecting binding data gain information about where users are active on the network, supplementing DHCP logs with more precise location information.

Care must be taken in attributing actions to users based on address binding information. While theoretically strong, administrators should allow for binding information being wrong and be cautious about actions based on apparent attribution. These techniques prevent spoofing from other sites entirely, so any attribution must account for possible external origin.
sections.eli5: Even with these checks, you still cannot be 100% sure who sent something without secret codes. These checks create privacy problems by recording who is where, so this information must be kept secret and deleted when it is not needed anymore.
